title: A computational status update for exact rational mixed integer programming
contribution: The journal version of the exact rational MIP status update: the 2013 hybrid-precision framework revised inside SCIP 7.0 with rational presolve (PaPILO), floating-point heuristics with exact repair, SoPlex iterative refinement, tighter integration and certificates for all bounding methods, studied one component at a time; on MIPLIB 2017 it solves 53 against 18 instances (10.7x on the 54 onesolved) and is 3.9x (reduced) and 8.1x (default) slower than floating-point SCIP on the 42 instances all three solve (pp. 1, 4-8, 17-18).
problem_entry: Roundoff compromises the optimality promise of floating-point MIP where MIP proves mathematics or verifies hardware (p. 2); the 2013 milestone framework lacks the supplementary techniques of floating-point solvers, so presolve (the component ranked highest in the literature) and heuristics (for usability) are added as 'a first step' (p. 2).
key_idea: Hybrid precision in every added component: rational presolve via templated PaPILO; heuristics on floating-point data with exact repair (fix the rounded integers, solve an exact LP); SoPlex refinement instead of QSopt_ex boosting; a padded objective limit; a running-error pre-check before exact feasibility checks; exact LPs at depths 4, 8, 16, ...; bound-shift off below 20% success (pp. 4-8, 10, 12).
assumptions: General MILP with rational data and a componentwise closest floating-point copy (p. 4); bound-shift needs bounds on all variables, project-and-shift an exact interior point or ray (p. 4); heuristics must not change the model (p. 5); repair off above 80% continuous variables (p. 14); certificates need presolve off (p. 15); test sets fpeasy (57), numdiff (50), the MIPLIB 2017 benchmark subset SCIP 7.0.2 solves in two hours (size not stated) and the full benchmark as 239 instances (pp. 9, 17).
proof_devices: running error analysis (Higham Alg. 3.2, adjusted for the roundoff in x* and a): s - mu >= b_j proves the row satisfied, s + mu <= b_j violated, otherwise exact recomputation; the adjusted bound is stated without proof (pp. 7-8, Algorithm 1)
objective limit padded by the average safe-bounding increase (at least 1e-6), with a re-solve without the limit when safe bounding fails (p. 7)

exact repair queue: improvement filter, 20% direct threshold with a buffer sorted by objective, hash table of processed integer assignments; off above 80% continuous variables; at most 1000 consecutive failures (pp. 5-6, 14)
rational presolve with identical acceptance thresholds and zero tolerances, transferred to SCIP through postsolve information (pp. 5, 13)
bound-shift off below 20% success; exact LP at depths 4, 8, 16, ...; project-and-shift no longer limited to fewer than 10000 nonzeros (pp. 10-12)
VIPR certificates extended to bound-shift, with dual multipliers computed in a postprocessing step (pp. 15-16)
experiments: Four numbered questions (p. 8). Xeon Gold 5122, CPLEX 12.3.0 for all, the predecessor's QSopt_ex or SoPlex 5.0.2, three seeds (one against the original), 7200 s, shift 0.001 s or 100 nodes (p. 9). One factor per table: framework with QSopt_ex fixed +7/+6/+15 solved (Table 1, pp. 9-10); SoPlex vs QSopt_ex +3/-6/+18 solved, time -59.2/-37.7/-60.1% (p. 12); presolve +6/+24/+13 solved at 0.6-1.3% of solving time (pp. 13-14); heuristics: time to first -79.7/-58.4/-97.2%, the numdiff gain partly variability (p. 15); certificates +56.3/+22/+46% on both-solved instances (p. 16); MIPLIB 2017: 53 vs 18 solved, 10.7x (p. 17); vs floating-point SCIP: 8.1x default, 3.9x reduced, 5.1x reduced on numdiff (pp. 17-18). My checks: '61 instances fewer' vs Table 11's 133 against 62 (pp. 17-18); 57.5% vs 57.6% (pp. 14-15); the parallel-presolve range omits numdiff (about 31%) (pp. 13-14); Table 8's caption vs the text (pp. 15-16); 239 vs 'complete' (p. 17); the count of discarded inconsistent instances is not printed (p. 17).
positioning: Revises and extends Cook-Koch-Steffy-Wolter 2013, 'The milestone paper', still the state of the art (p. 2), and critiques it by evidence (a likely performance bug, fn. 1, p. 11; incorrect root reasoning on x_4, p. 16); surveys roundoff avoidance by community (Concorde, SAT/PBO, SMT, polyhedral libraries, hybrid LP methods, safe bounds) with SAT proof checking as the rigor model (pp. 3-4); price of exactness set against Wolter's thesis (p. 17); no other exact MIP code is run; 10 of 37 references include Gleixner (pp. 19-20).
writing: The abstract opens on the predecessor and ends on 10.7x and 2.9 times as many solved without naming the 54-instance subset (pp. 1, 17); scope-modest ('a first step', 'a first, small selection of methods', pp. 2-3); attributions hedged one by one ('may be', 'most likely', 'seems to be', 'This hypothesis is supported', pp. 11, 17-18); expectations written before measurement (pp. 6, 13); 'slight decrease' for a 24% drop (p. 13); typos (pp. 5, 6, 13, 18).
limits_future: The gap to floating-point solvers is 'still large' (8.1x default, 3.9x reduced), with the missing techniques named (cuts, propagation, conflict analysis, symmetry) (pp. 17-18); refinement breaks down on ill-conditioned LPs, so chip-verification instances are lost (pp. 7, 12); presolve is not certified (p. 15); future: numerically safe cuts, precision boosting inside SoPlex, VIPR certificates for presolve (p. 18).

method_links.note: Floating-point SCIP 7.0.1 at default and in a reduced setting without the features exact SCIP lacks; both factors printed (8.1 and 3.9 on the 42 instances all three solve) with the attribution to missing solving methods; CPLEX 12.3.0 and the predecessor's QSopt_ex for all experiments (step 5); Table 1 holds the exact LP solver fixed; a gain from the predecessor's likely performance bug printed (step 9, fn. 1); the predecessor's sets reused plus MIPLIB 2017 (step 7), and Wolter's price-of-exactness numbers re-measured on the shared numdiff set (5.1 against 9.16).

The SCIP 3.0 vs 7.0 base difference is argued away, not measured (p. 9); inconsistent instances are discarded from Table 11 without a count (p. 17); the text's '61 instances fewer' contradicts Table 11's 133 against 62, the slip SKILL.md notes; SKILL.md's step-4 quote sits on printed p. 809 (file p. 17), not 810.

Each printed limit carries a cause and a next project: chip-verification losses from refinement breakdown -> precision boosting inside SoPlex; the still-large gap, now with factors -> numerically safe cuts (ref. [15]); presolve outside the certificates -> VIPR output for presolve; bound-shift time per call -> future code versions. Step 5 (a lost experiment read as the next idea), cited in SKILL.md from automatic captions [MIP21], is here in print.

In print the SoPlex switch lost 6 numdiff observations (all chip verification) but gained 3 on fpeasy and 18 on miplib (Table 3), not 'as many hard instances as it won' as step 5's talk paraphrase has it.

Certificates extended to bound-shift; coverage printed (presolve must be disabled because PaPILO cannot yet produce certificates); on x_4 a certificate exposed incorrect root reasoning (a bound beyond the solver's infinity value) behind a correct infeasibility verdict; overhead measured on both-solved instances with the timeout bias stated; checking cheaper than solving; verifying the whole solve named as the goal.

The journal's certificate overheads (+56.3%/+22%/+46% solving time; 92.5/32.8/65.8% with checking, Table 9) differ without comment from the IPCO +101.2%/+51.4% that step 6 quotes [ZR21-04]; the journal says they confirm VIPR 2017 (ref. [13]). Step 6 and Method 3's forecast counter-evidence should name the version they rest on.

Heuristics exclusively on the floating-point approximation with exact repair; a running-error pre-check with exact recomputation only in the undecided band; a padded objective limit with a fallback re-solve; bound-shift off below 20%; exact LPs at depths 4, 8, 16, ...; repair filters and failure limits; model-changing presolve fully rational at 0.6-1.3% of solving time (step 1). The Limitations line (no reliable recovery when the floating-point LP fails) is printed here: SoPlex relies on double-precision simplex solves, and the chip-verification trees blow up.

Step 9 in practice: instances feasible within tolerances but infeasible in exact arithmetic are discarded from the floating-point comparison, and a 1000-failure limit guards the repair heuristic against them.

The beliefs measured are open transfers rather than field folklore: whether the LP-level 5.5x of refinement carries over to MIP re-solves (two reasons for doubt given), and whether rational presolve finds more or fewer reductions (mechanisms both ways); each gets its own table.

Between versions the closing sentence 'the performance gap to floating-point solvers is still large' gains its numbers: D002 had no floating-point baseline (card in c10), the journal backs it with 8.1x default, 3.9x reduced and 5.1x reduced on numdiff.
The adjective survives next to a count: 'slight decrease' for numdiff fixings 46.8 -> 35.5 and aggregations 52.2 -> 40.0 (24% and 23%), as in D002.

Count correction: the journal's computational section opens with 'four main questions' (the fourth is the floating-point comparison); SKILL.md says three for [SU23]; three is the IPCO version D002 (card in c10).

Heuristics are judged by time to the first solution and the primal integral, 'established measures of primal performance', and motivated by usability: 'finding good solutions earlier may be more relevant than proving optimality eventually'.

Instance-seed pairs as observations with three seeds; overheads on both-solved instances with the timeout bias stated; arithmetic vs geometric means by normalization on the subset where both variants ran a method; the two excluded infeasible instances named and the gain restated without them.
The abstract's 10.7x does not name its 54-instance subset; inconsistent instances are discarded from Table 11 without a count; Table 8's caption and the text name different instance sets.
PaPILO is 'fully templatized with respect to the arithmetic type', which lets exact SCIP run its presolve in rational arithmetic.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Heuristics should not speed up infeasible instances; the numdiff gain (-18.9%) partly came from alu10_1 and alu16_2, which were rerun with 10 seeds (the effect mostly gone on alu16_2, persistent on alu10_1), and the gain was restated without them (13%), the cause given as solver decisions that the seed does not reach.

Framework revision with the exact LP solver fixed (Table 1), then SoPlex vs QSopt_ex (Tables 3-4), presolve (Tables 5-6), heuristics (Tables 7-8), certificates (Table 9), all-on vs the original (Table 10), and floating-point SCIP at default and reduced (Tables 11-12); D002 (card in c10) has the same order with fewer steps.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: attribute a speed-up by nodes against time per node
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Time cuts on fpeasy and miplib track the node cuts, and the only change expected to cut nodes is the interleaved exact LP; node-processing time barely moves (0.101 vs 0.115 on miplib); the gained instances are traced to the removed project-and-shift limit (4 of 6 on numdiff, 9 on miplib).

'61 instances fewer' vs Table 11's 133 against 62; repair success 57.5% in the text vs 57.6% in Table 7; the parallel-presolve range '38.9% (fpeasy) to 43.7% (miplib)' omits numdiff's 0.49 -> 0.34 s; Table 8's caption and the text name different instance sets (as in D002); the 'complete' benchmark set vs 239 instances in Table 10 (240 in D002 per c10).

transferable: Staircase study: one factor per table on top of the previous configuration, then all-on against the predecessor and against the fast solver at default and reduced (pp. 8-18).
Attribute a speed-up by decomposition: nodes against time per node, the node cut tied to the only change that can cause it, the gained instances traced to the removed restriction (pp. 10-11).
Negative control: if a component seems to help where it cannot (heuristics on infeasible instances), rerun those instances with 10 seeds, name them, and restate the gain without them (p. 15, fn. 2).

Exact repair queue for approximate heuristic solutions: fix the integers and solve an exact LP behind an improvement filter, a 20% direct threshold with a buffer sorted by objective and a hash of integer assignments; off above 80% continuous variables and after 1000 consecutive failures (pp. 5-6, 14).
Safe floating-point pre-check by running error analysis, with exact recomputation only for the undecided band |s - b_j| < mu (pp. 7-8).
Pad an approximate LP's objective cutoff by the average observed safe-bounding increase (at least 1e-6), and re-solve without it when safe bounding fails (p. 7).
Compare exact and floating-point versions of a component with identical acceptance thresholds and zero tolerances; report the reductions as well as the time, with count means shifted by 1 (p. 13).
Before measuring, write down why the effect could go either way (p. 13).
When a factor differs from a predecessor's, re-measure on the set both studies used and explain the difference there (pp. 17-18).

quotes.text: Besides ensuring correctness of results, certificate generation is valuable to ensure correctness of the solver.
We have to attribute a portion of the speedup on numdiff to performance variability since some of the instances where the variant with enabled heuristics is much faster are two infeasible instances.
